title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
source_work: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
spine: Utterson follows the evidence of Hyde’s crimes toward the locked cabinet, while Jekyll’s divided self destroys the life Utterson is trying to protect.
logline: When a respectable London lawyer discovers that a brutal stranger is protected by his friend Dr. Jekyll, he pursues the connection through murder, secrecy and scientific horror until breaking into Jekyll’s cabinet reveals the truth—and Jekyll’s confession shows the catastrophe from within.

slug.location_name: Black Mail House door and adjoining by-street
slug.text: EXT. BLACK MAIL HOUSE DOOR AND ADJOINING BY-STREET - DAY

elements.text: A Sunday street glitters with polished brass and fresh paint. Then the brightness breaks.
A blind, discoloured wall thrusts over a single door. No bell. No knocker. The panels are blistered and blackened by match-strikes.
MR. RICHARD ENFIELD, 50s, his cane polished from constant use, points across the street.
Did you ever remark that door?
It is connected in my mind … with a very odd story.
GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, a lawyer's gloves folded in one hand, stops beside him.
Indeed? … and what was that?
Enfield gives him the story: a little man tramples a child and leaves her screaming. The people catch him. He offers a hundred pounds to make the matter disappear.
The door stands behind Enfield. Its lock remains clean beneath the grime.
If you choose to make capital out of this accident … I am naturally helpless. No gentleman but wishes to avoid a scene … Name your figure.
Set your mind at rest … I will stay with you till the banks open and cash the cheque myself.
Utterson's hand closes around his cane. The tale has become a document.
Black Mail House is what I call the place with the door … Though even that, you know, is far from explaining all.
And you don’t know if the drawer of the cheque lives there?
Enfield's cane lowers toward the door, but does not touch it.
I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.
There is no other door, and nobody goes in or out of that one but, once in a great while, the gentleman of my adventure.
A key turns somewhere beyond the wall. The sound stops them.
I want to ask the name of that man who walked over the child.
It was a man of the name of Hyde.
What sort of a man is he to see?
There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something down-right detestable.
The door opens. EDWARD HYDE, 30s, a cheque folded inside his glove, emerges and locks it behind him.
The fact is, if I do not ask you the name of the other party, it is because I know it already.
Utterson takes the cheque. The signature is visible before Hyde can fold it away: JEKYLL.
The fellow had a key; and what’s more, he has it still. I saw him use it not a week ago.
Let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.
Utterson folds the cheque into his coat instead of returning it.
With all my heart … I shake hands on that, Richard.
Their hands part. Utterson stays facing the locked door.

elements.text: GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, a silver watch-chain crossing his waistcoat, walks beside the neglected door. RICHARD ENFIELD, 40s, his cane tucked beneath one arm, lifts it toward the entry.
Did you ever remark that door?
It is connected in my mind … with a very odd story.
Indeed? … and what was that?
Enfield's cane settles against the locked wood. He does not touch the handle.
Well, it was this way … I was coming home from some place at the end of the world, about three o’clock of a black winter morning …
The story takes shape between them: a little man collides with a girl, then tramples calmly over her. Enfield's cane lifts from the door.
If you choose to make capital out of this accident … I am naturally helpless. No gentleman but wishes to avoid a scene … Name your figure.
A cheque appears in Enfield's hand. Its signature is turned away from us.
Set your mind at rest … I will stay with you till the banks open and cash the cheque myself.
The cheque changes hands. Enfield folds it before the signature can be read.
Utterson stops beside the door. The street carries on around him.
Black Mail House is what I call the place with the door … Though even that, you know, is far from explaining all.
And you don’t know if the drawer of the cheque lives there?
Enfield points past the door, toward the blank upper windows. No face appears behind them.
I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.
There is no other door, and nobody goes in or out of that one but, once in a great while, the gentleman of my adventure.
Enfield … that’s a good rule of yours.
Utterson takes the folded cheque from his pocket. He keeps it between two fingers, as if it might stain.
I want to ask the name of that man who walked over the child.
It was a man of the name of Hyde.
What sort of a man is he to see?
There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something down-right detestable.
Utterson turns the cheque over. The name on its face is now visible to him.
The fact is, if I do not ask you the name of the other party, it is because I know it already.
The fellow had a key; and what’s more, he has it still. I saw him use it not a week ago.
Utterson folds the cheque along the respectable signature. He puts it away.
Let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.
With all my heart … I shake hands on that, Richard.
They shake hands. Behind them, the locked door remains shut.

elements.text: MR. GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, a lawyer's gloves folded in one hand, walks beside Mr. Richard Enfield.
Enfield lifts his cane toward the neglected door.
Did you ever remark that door?
It is connected in my mind … with a very odd story.
Indeed? … and what was that?
The door has no sign. Its windows above are shut and clean. A chimney smokes behind the packed buildings.
Well, it was this way … I was coming home from some place at the end of the world, about three o’clock of a black winter morning …
A small figure collides with a running girl at the corner. He tramples calmly over her and keeps walking.
Enfield catches him and drags him back through the gathering crowd.
If you choose to make capital out of this accident … I am naturally helpless. No gentleman but wishes to avoid a scene … Name your figure.
Later, Hyde returns through the door with gold in one hand and a cheque in the other.
Set your mind at rest … I will stay with you till the banks open and cash the cheque myself.
Enfield's thumb covers the signature as he holds the cheque out. The name beneath it remains visible to Utterson.
Black Mail House is what I call the place with the door … Though even that, you know, is far from explaining all.
And you don’t know if the drawer of the cheque lives there?
A likely place, isn’t it? … But I happen to have noticed his address; he lives in some square or other.
And you never asked about the—place with the door?
No, sir; I had a delicacy. I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.
Utterson stops beside the door. The cheque is still between them.
I want to ask the name of that man who walked over the child.
It was a man of the name of Hyde.
What sort of a man is he to see?
There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something down-right detestable.
Utterson's hand closes over the cheque. He has heard the name before.
The fact is, if I do not ask you the name of the other party, it is because I know it already.
You see, Richard, your tale has gone home. If you have been inexact in any point you had better correct it.
The fellow had a key; and what’s more, he has it still. I saw him use it not a week ago.
Enfield points at the lock. The keyhole is polished bright against the neglected paint.
Let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.
Utterson extends his hand. The cheque disappears into his coat.
With all my heart … I shake hands on that, Richard.

slug.text: INT. MR. UTTERSON’S HOUSE AND CHAMBERS - DAY

elements.text: GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, a candle burning beside his locked safe.
He removes Jekyll’s will. The name EDWARD HYDE fills the page.
I thought it was madness … and now I begin to fear it is disgrace.
The will disappears into the safe. Utterson turns the key twice.
Night. A bed under drawn curtains. Utterson lies awake until the dark gives way to morning.
In a by-street of shops, he takes up a watch beside Jekyll’s door.
If he be Mr. Hyde, … I shall be Mr. Seek.
Footsteps. Light, quick, approaching.
Utterson slips into the court entry. EDWARD HYDE, 30s, a key already in hand, crosses toward the door.
Mr. Hyde, I think?
That is my name. What do you want?
I see you are going in. I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might admit me.
You will not find Dr. Jekyll; he is from home … How did you know me?
Hyde blows across the key. He keeps it between them.
On your side, … will you do me a favour?
With pleasure, … What shall it be?
Will you let me see your face?
Hyde turns. Defiance replaces the lowered face. The two men hold each other’s gaze.
Now I shall know you again. It may be useful.
Yes, … it is as well we have met; and à propos, you should have my address.
Hyde gives him a Soho address. Then his hand finds the lock.
And now, … how did you know me?
By description.
Whose description?
We have common friends, …
Common friends, … Who are they?
Jekyll, for instance, …
He never told you. I did not think you would have lied.
The lock turns. Hyde vanishes through the door before Utterson can follow.
Later that night, Utterson knocks at Jekyll’s house. POOLE, 60s, an immaculate servant with a ring of household keys, opens the door.
I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room, Poole. Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is from home?
Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir. Mr. Hyde has a key.
Utterson’s hand closes around the iron rail beside the door.
Your master seems to repose a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole, …
Yes, sir, he does indeed. We have all orders to obey him.
I do not think I ever met Mr. Hyde?
O, dear no, sir. He never dines here. Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.
Beyond Poole, the passage to the laboratory stands unlit.
Well, good-night, Poole.
Good-night, Mr. Utterson.
The door closes. Utterson walks home alone, the Soho address folded in his pocket.
Poor Harry Jekyll, … my mind misgives me he is in deep waters!
He stops beneath a gas lamp. The address remains unopened in his hand.
Ah, I must put my shoulder to the wheel—if Jekyll will but let me. If Jekyll will only let me.

Later. A dark bed. Utterson lies awake beneath the curtains.
By day, he keeps watch in the by-street. By night, he returns.

Footsteps. Light. Near.

Well, good-night, Poole.
Good-night, Mr. Utterson.
Utterson steps into the night. The laboratory door remains behind him.
Poor Harry Jekyll, … my mind misgives me he is in deep waters!

elements.text: GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, his nightshirt buttoned beneath a dressing gown, lies awake in the dark.
Church bells strike six. He throws back the covers.
A street of shuttered shops. Utterson keeps watch beside a court entrance, morning after morning.
A light footstep approaches. Utterson slips into the entry.
EDWARD HYDE, 30s, a key already in hand, crosses toward Jekyll’s door.
Mr. Hyde, I think?
That is my name. What do you want?
Hyde blows on the key. He does not offer it.
I see you are going in. I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might admit me.
You will not find Dr. Jekyll; he is from home … How did you know me?
On your side, … will you do me a favour?
With pleasure, … What shall it be?
Will you let me see your face?
Hyde turns. Defiance replaces courtesy. The two men hold each other’s gaze.
Now I shall know you again. It may be useful.
Yes, … it is as well we have met; and à propos, you should have my address.
Hyde gives him a Soho address, then fits the key to the lock.
And now, … how did you know me?
By description.
Whose description?
We have common friends, …
Common friends, … Who are they?
Jekyll, for instance, …
He never told you. I did not think you would have lied.
The lock turns. Hyde vanishes through the door before Utterson can follow.
Utterson remains at the threshold, the Soho address folded in his hand.
That night, he knocks at Jekyll’s house. POOLE, 60s, a servant’s key-ring heavy at his waist, opens the hall door.
I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room, Poole. Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is from home?
Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir. Mr. Hyde has a key.
Utterson’s hand closes over the folded address.
Your master seems to repose a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole, …
Yes, sir, he does indeed. We have all orders to obey him.
The servant’s keys hang between them. Beyond the hall, the passage to the laboratory stands unlit.
I do not think I ever met Mr. Hyde?
O, dear no, sir. He never dines here. Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.
Well, good-night, Poole.
Good-night, Mr. Utterson.
Outside, Utterson walks home alone. He does not unfold the address.
Poor Harry Jekyll, … my mind misgives me he is in deep waters!
He pockets the address and turns toward home.

elements.text: GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, coat buttoned against the frost, keeps watch outside the black door.
The street is empty. A single set of footsteps approaches.
Utterson slips into the court entry.
EDWARD HYDE, 20s, small and plainly dressed, crosses toward the door. He draws a key.
Mr. Hyde, I think?
Utterson touches his shoulder. Hyde recoils with a sharp intake of breath.
That is my name. What do you want?
I see you are going in. I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might admit me.
Hyde blows on the key without looking up.
You will not find Dr. Jekyll; he is from home … How did you know me?
On your side, … will you do me a favour?
With pleasure, … What shall it be?
Will you let me see your face?
Hyde hesitates. Then he turns and faces Utterson.
They stare at each other. Hyde gives him a number in Soho.
Now I shall know you again. It may be useful.
Yes, … it is as well we have met; and à propos, you should have my address.
And now, … how did you know me?
By description.
Whose description?
We have common friends, …
Common friends, … Who are they?
Jekyll, for instance, …
He never told you. I did not think you would have lied.
Hyde snarls a laugh, unlocks the door, and vanishes inside.
If he be Mr. Hyde, … I shall be Mr. Seek.
Later, Utterson stands in Jekyll’s hall. POOLE, 60s, a household key-ring at his waist, opens the door.
I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room, Poole. Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is from home?
Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir. Mr. Hyde has a key.
The key-ring at Poole’s waist remains still.
Your master seems to repose a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole, …
Yes, sir, he does indeed. We have all orders to obey him.
I do not think I ever met Mr. Hyde?
O, dear no, sir. He never dines here. Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.
Beyond the hall, the laboratory door stands closed.
Well, good-night, Poole.
Good-night, Mr. Utterson.
Utterson walks home beneath the lamps, one hand pressed to his brow.
Poor Harry Jekyll, … my mind misgives me he is in deep waters!

slug.text: INT. DR. JEKYLL’S HOUSE AND LABORATORY - NIGHT

elements.text: GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, his legal papers locked behind him, sits awake in the darkness.
He opens the safe. Removes Jekyll’s will. The words naming Edward Hyde wait on the page.
I thought it was madness … and now I begin to fear it is disgrace.
Night after night, the same by-street. Utterson waits near the black door.
A light footstep approaches. Utterson slips into the court entry.
EDWARD HYDE, 30s, a key already in hand, crosses toward the door as if coming home.
Mr. Hyde, I think?
That is my name. What do you want?
I see you are going in. I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might admit me.
You will not find Dr. Jekyll; he is from home … How did you know me?
On your side, … will you do me a favour?
With pleasure, … What shall it be?
Will you let me see your face?
Hyde turns. Defiance fixes his face. The two men hold each other’s gaze.
Now I shall know you again. It may be useful.
Yes, … it is as well we have met; and à propos, you should have my address.
Hyde gives him a Soho number, then turns the key.
And now, … how did you know me?
By description.
Whose description?
We have common friends, …
Common friends, … Who are they?
Jekyll, for instance, …
He never told you. I did not think you would have lied.
The key turns. Hyde vanishes through Jekyll’s door before Utterson can follow.
Later, in Jekyll’s hall, POOLE, 60s, a servant’s white gloves immaculate, opens the door.
I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room, Poole. Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is from home?
Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir. Mr. Hyde has a key.
Your master seems to repose a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole, …
Yes, sir, he does indeed. We have all orders to obey him.
Utterson’s hand leaves the fender. He has the answer he came for, and it opens a worse question.
I do not think I ever met Mr. Hyde?
O, dear no, sir. He never dines here. Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.
Well, good-night, Poole.
Utterson steps into the night. Behind him, the laboratory entrance remains shut.
Poor Harry Jekyll, … my mind misgives me he is in deep waters!

elements.text: GABRIEL JOHN UTTERSON, 50s, a candle guttering beside his open safe.
He removes Jekyll’s will. The name HYDE catches the candlelight.
I thought it was madness … and now I begin to fear it is disgrace.
The will goes back into the safe. The lock turns.
Night after night, Utterson keeps watch in the by-street. Shop shutters close. His candle burns low.
If he be Mr. Hyde, … I shall be Mr. Seek.
A light footstep approaches. Utterson withdraws into the court entry.
EDWARD HYDE, 30s, a key already drawn for Jekyll’s door.
Mr. Hyde, I think?
That is my name. What do you want?
I see you are going in. I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might admit me.
You will not find Dr. Jekyll; he is from home … How did you know me?
Hyde blows on the key. Utterson steps into his path.
On your side, … will you do me a favour?
With pleasure, … What shall it be?
Will you let me see your face?
Hyde turns. Defiance replaces concealment. They hold each other’s gaze.
Now I shall know you again. It may be useful.
Yes, … it is as well we have met; and à propos, you should have my address.
Hyde gives him a Soho address, then unlocks Jekyll’s door.
And now, … how did you know me?
By description.
Whose description?
We have common friends, …
Common friends, … Who are they?
Jekyll, for instance, …
He never told you. I did not think you would have lied.
The door shuts between them.
At Jekyll’s house, POole opens the hall door. UTTERSON does not remove his coat.
I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room, Poole. Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is from home?
Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir. Mr. Hyde has a key.
Utterson’s hand closes around the will in his pocket.
Your master seems to repose a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole, …
Yes, sir, he does indeed. We have all orders to obey him.
I do not think I ever met Mr. Hyde?
O, dear no, sir. He never dines here. Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.
Beyond the hall, the laboratory door stands shut.
Well, good-night, Poole.
Good-night, Mr. Utterson.
Utterson walks home. The key, the orders, and the laboratory door follow him through the dark.
Poor Harry Jekyll, … my mind misgives me he is in deep waters!
He stops beneath a streetlamp. The will remains in his pocket.
Ah, I must put my shoulder to the wheel—if Jekyll will but let me,” he added, “if Jekyll will only let me.
